Read governing rules for merge force + approvals (r-gemini-key-load, r-task-phase-needs-wave) and the consume/approvals sites; the fix follows the single-use digest-bound approval contract.
Split approval check (consume.check, no spend) from spend; merge_force.authorise validates only; merge spends via merge_force.spend after W.merge lands.

chunk_findings.detail: `check` performs only a non-reserving read: two interleaved callers with the same single-use `ask_id` can both get `Decision.ok` before either `spend` records `ask.consumed`. Both callers may then perform their guarded side effect; the first `spend` consumes the approval and the second `spend` fails only after its side effect has already happened, defeating the single-use guarantee. The old `spend` checked and recorded under one `log.transaction()` and would have refused the losing caller before the side effect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: `spend` returns `CN.spend(log, canon_of(log, item, a), approval).stamp` without checking the result’s `ok`/`message` fields, even though `authorise` immediately above treats `CN.check` as a fallible result. Because `authorise` no longer consumes the approval before landing, `spend` is the point that must still enforce the single-use guarantee. A concrete interleaving: two concurrent `merge --force --approval A` invocations on different worktrees both pass `CN.check` while `A` is unused, both git landings succeed, and the first `CN.spend` consumes `A`. The second `CN.spend` now sees an already-consumed approval and returns a non-ok result, but this function still returns its `.stamp` (typically `None`) instead of propagating the refusal. The second merge is then recorded as forced with no valid single-use approval, or the caller emits a `merge.forced` event with a bogus proof.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/merge_force.py:spend

chunk_findings.detail: `check` validates a single-use approval with no lock and no reservation, and `spend` only appends `ask.consumed` later. Two callers that share one `ask_id` and canon can both pass `check`, both finish a git landing, and only the first `spend` records a use: the second landing is already on the branch when `spend` returns `Decision(False, ...)`. `merge` then does `forced_by = MF.spend(...)` and still calls `_record_forced` with no check of that result, so one approval authorizes two forced landings (or a landed merge is followed by a failed spend and a bad forced stamp). The same window fails a slow landing whose approval expires after `check` and before `spend`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: `check` validates the approval without taking `log.transaction()` and without creating any reservation or token, while `spend` later re-runs `_checked` from scratch with a fresh clock/log read. Given the single-use approval this bug targets, Process A and Process B can both call `check` successfully before either calls `spend`; both perform their side effect (e.g. the git landing), then A's `spend` appends `ask.consumed`. B's `spend` now sees the consumed event and returns `Decision(False, ...)`, but B's side effect has already occurred. The same gap occurs sequentially if the ask expires between `check` and `spend`: `spend` reads the new time and refuses after the caller has already landed, leaving the side effect performed with no recorded `ask.consumed`. This breaks the single-use invariant that the original `spend` enforced atomically under `log.transaction()`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: A single-use approval is only checked in `_override` and not claimed/consumed until after the git merge has already landed. Between those two points the approval can expire or be consumed by a concurrent request, and `MF.spend` will then fail; `_spend_after_land` returns a non-stamp `{"ask": approval, "note": spent.message}`, but the branch is already merged and the caller proceeds to `_record_forced`. For example, a short-lived approval passes `MF.authorise`, a post-merge hook stalls past the approval expiry, git lands successfully, and `MF.spend` fails; the merge remains even though the single-use approval was never validly spent. This lets an expired or concurrently consumed approval still produce a landed merge without valid authorization.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py:_spend_after_land (call at :339)

chunk_findings.detail: The split between `authorise`’s non-spending `CN.check` and the post-landing `CN.spend` is a TOCTOU. Interleaving: process A starts `merge.force --approval X`, `authorise` passes `CN.check` without spending; process B consumes the same single-use approval; process A’s git landing then succeeds; A calls `spend`, and `CN.spend` returns `Decision.ok == False` (the docstring itself acknowledges this can happen). At that point the merge has already landed, but the caller must not record a `merge.forced` proof, so users get either a failed command after a successful merge, or a landed merge with no valid `merge.forced` event. The new tests only cover the sequential path and do not cover this interleaving, so the change does not preserve the invariant it is fixing.

chunk_findings.detail: `check()` validates a single-use approval outside any lock or reservation, and `spend()` only records the use later. Two concurrent forced merges using the same `ask_id` can both call `check()` and get `Decision(ok=True)` before either records `ask.consumed`; both then perform their side effects. The first `spend()` succeeds, but the second `spend()` re-validates under the lock, sees the approval already consumed, and returns `Decision(ok=False)` after that second landing has already happened. A single-use approval thus authorizes two side effects and the second caller is left with a refused spend after its side effect. This reintroduces a lost-update between validation and consumption that the old atomic `spend()` prevented.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: The new `authorise`/`spend` split is a time-of-check to time-of-use gap with no reservation: `authorise` only runs `CN.check`, and the single use is recorded later by `CN.spend`. If the approval expires, or another consumer spends it, after `authorise` succeeds but before the landing reaches `spend`, git has already landed but `spend` returns `.ok == False` (the docstring itself lists expiry as a failure). The caller cannot un-land git, so the command either reports failure for a merge that did land, or records a landed merge without the required single-use proof. The old path consumed before any irreversible git action.

chunk_findings.detail: The new function is annotated `-> dict[str, Any]`, but its body returns `CN.spend(...)`, which is documented as `CN`'s `Decision` object whose callers access `.ok` (and `authorise` already accesses `d.ok`, `d.stamp`, `d.message`). A caller that trusts the annotation and does `MF.spend(...)["ok"]` gets a `TypeError`, and a static type checker will flag the implementation or callers.
